Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

flexCountReg 0.1.2 (development)

Count probabilities and intervals for every estimator

  • predict(type = "prob") takes counts, the counts to evaluate (such as 0:10, 5:8 or c(0, 1, 10)), besides max_count (short for 0:max_count). Only those counts are evaluated. underflow = TRUE adds the probability below the smallest count, as overflow = TRUE does above the largest. counts also works for countreg_mv() ("prob" and "conditional") and the finite mixtures.
  • type = "prob" for countreg_rp(), countreg_fe(), countreg_hier(), renb(), repois(), poislind_re() and negmultinom(): the marginal distribution of a count of a new unit, with its random terms integrated out (countreg_fe(): given the estimated group effect; countreg_hier(): given the estimated effects, or marginal with marginal = TRUE). rootogram() works for these models too, and for countreg_mv() draws one rootogram per outcome (outcome selects some of them).
  • countreg_alloc(): type = "total_prob" and "count_prob" give the count probabilities of the total and of each category.
  • Confidence and prediction intervals (interval =) for every estimator except countreg_fe(), whose group effects have no covariance matrix. Models with several outcomes return a list of data frames. In a simulation with 10 models (150 replications, level 0.90), the confidence intervals covered 0.86 to 0.93 of the true means and the prediction intervals 0.94 to 0.99 of new counts (discrete counts make them conservative).
  • Rows with a missing covariate have NA probabilities in hurdle models (where P(0) was returned) and countreg_mv() models (where they were 0).
  • margEffTable() works for countreg_alloc() models: effects on the expected count of each category and on the total, with standard errors (it averaged over the categories, without standard errors).
  • New fit_resamples_counts(): resamples workflows or specifications with several outcomes, which tune::fit_resamples() cannot, and computes the out-of-sample log score of the count distribution for any engine.

tidymodels

  • count_reg() has every estimator as an engine: "flexCountReg" (countreg()), "countreg_rp", "countreg_mix", "countreg_lc", "countreg_fe", "countreg_hier", "countreg_alloc", "countreg_mv", "renb", "repois", "poislind_re" and "negmultinom". New article vignette("tidymodels").
  • New prediction types: "conf_int" and "pred_int" (all engines except "countreg_fe") and "raw", whose opts reach every option of predict(). The engine argument predict_args sets predict() options for numeric predictions and intervals; fit_engine is the estimators’ engine.
  • Tuning works: count_reg() had no update() method, so every tune_grid() and finalize_workflow() failed. New tuning parameters count_components(), count_zero_type(), count_correlated() and count_re_dist().
  • rmse() and mae() no longer break yardstick when flexCountReg is loaded after it: with a data frame they call the yardstick metric, and they work in metric_set().
  • Without a model formula (a recipe or add_formula()), columns named in offset, group_var, panel_id, cluster, fixef, cre_group or time (and the variables of rpar_formula with "countreg_rp") no longer enter the mean model. The documentation wrongly said that columns with a non-predictor role reach the model; it now describes what works.
  • Case weights that are not whole numbers give a warning unless weight_type is set (the previous warning for importance weights never appeared, because parsnip passes only their values).
  • Models extracted from tidymodels fits work with update() (which now also has a method for them) and with bootstrap refits when flexCountReg is not attached. Their stored call holds the argument values.
  • predict() for countreg_alloc(), countreg_mv() and countreg_hier() models accepts new_data; it was ignored, so the predictions were those of the training data.
  • augment() methods for countreg_alloc() and countreg_mv().

Corrections from the November 2026 review

A review of the whole package found the following problems, now fixed, each with a regression test.

Estimates and inference

  • Random-parameter models (countreg_alloc(), countreg_mv(), correlated random parameters in countreg_mix() / countreg_lc()): flipping Cholesky columns after the fit to report positive standard deviations now flips the stored simulation draws too (for mixtures, each class’s own draws), so the reported estimates, log-likelihood, scores, Hessian, robust standard errors and posterior weights all belong to the simulated optimum. Before, the log-likelihood at the reported estimates could be lower than the reported maximum (by about 1 to 4 in the review’s examples).
  • countreg_mv() copulas: probabilities of counts in the upper tails of their distributions (and other rows whose copula corners cancel) are now integrated over the upper-tail probabilities instead of differenced near 1, keeping their relative precision with analytic gradients. Such rows used to collapse to probability 0 and could distort the fitted dependence (one extreme pair in independent data gave a Frank theta of -6.56). Joint and conditional predictions use the same computation.
  • countreg_alloc() and countreg_mv() with random parameters: frequency weights now multiply each unit’s log-likelihood (they entered inside the simulated average, so rescaling the weights changed the estimates). With group_var, weights must be constant within units.
  • countreg_alloc() with truncated = TRUE: predict(type = "total_positive") and conditional = TRUE with random parameters now average E(c | b) / (1 - P0(b)) over the random parameters, as the likelihood implies; simulate() with a shared site-year term redraws the shared term with each rejected total (it sampled a different distribution and could leave zero totals).
  • Predictions that integrate over random parameters (countreg_alloc(), countreg_mv(), the mixtures’ count probabilities and moments) use Gauss-Hermite grids (exact for the lognormal means of normal random parameters) instead of plain Halton points, which reach only about three standard deviations and biased expected counts by 1-4%. Mixture component means are exact (from the moment generating function) when the family’s mean is proportional to mu, and Inf with a warning where the expected count does not exist (a lognormal random parameter with a positive covariate, or a gamma random parameter with large variance), as in countreg_rp(); margEffTable() then stops with a clear message.
  • Mixture bootstrap refits normalize the signs of the random-parameter scales before label alignment; posterior class probabilities of the training data are the same with and without newdata.
  • repois() uses its analytic score in the optimizer, the stored scores and the final Hessian (its standard errors came from numerical derivatives and were off by up to a factor of three with panel weights); poislind_re() gains an analytic score, so its standard errors are accurate.
  • The Poisson-Weibull distribution (dpoisweibull(), ppoisweibull(), family = "PW") no longer returns Inf, NaN or probabilities above 1 for large or very small Weibull shapes; the quadrature finds the peak of the integrand with a bracketed search and checks its own accuracy.
  • DPO and GAMMACOUNT: the mean equation is solved across the documented shape range (the probability was 0 below a shape of about 0.003-0.005); DPO also needs mu / phi below about 1e10 (documented).
  • countreg_fe(): groups whose observations, counting frequency weights, number one are dropped as single observations (the rule counted rows, so weighted fits differed from the expanded data); predict(newgroup = "mean_fe") uses a fixed mean of the estimated effects (weighted by the groups’ sizes) instead of one that depended on the other rows of newdata.
  • Cluster-robust covariances of panel models whose panels each have one row match scores to rows by panel id (they could be assigned to the wrong panel).

Errors and crashes

  • Factors with unused levels (after subsetting, after rows with missing values are dropped, or declared) no longer stop estimation with a “rank deficient” error: as in lm(), unused levels are dropped in every formula, including random-effect terms of countreg_hier().
  • vcov(type = "robust") works for countreg_fe() fits (the groups are the units for the conditional and concentrated likelihoods).
  • cbind(...) ~ . works in countreg_alloc() and no longer uses the other outcomes as predictors in countreg_mv() (the . stands for the columns other than the counts).
  • temporal_effects() and temporal_tests() work for countreg_mv() fits (with an outcome column), for tv(basis = "smooth") with any mgcv basis, and for tv(1, time = ...) in rpar_formula without a fixed intercept; smooths written with s() are no longer reported as time-varying effects, and a tv() term inside an interaction gives a clear message instead of being ignored.
  • margEffTable() works for countreg_mv() fits (effects on each outcome’s mean) and no longer reports an effect for the time variable of tv(basis = "smooth").

Simulation for every estimator

  • simulate() (for parametric bootstrapping) now works for countreg_rp(), renb(), repois(), poislind_re(), negmultinom() and countreg_fe(), which refused it before; with countreg(), countreg_hier(), the mixtures, countreg_alloc() and countreg_mv() every estimator simulates. Each simulation draws the model’s random terms anew: each unit’s random coefficients (countreg_rp(), one draw per panel or row, with correlations and heterogeneity in means and variances), each panel’s random effect (beta for renb(), gamma for repois() and negmultinom(), Lindley for poislind_re()), or the counts given the estimated fixed effects (countreg_fe()). Simulated means equal the models’ expected counts, panels share their effects, and refits on simulated data recover the parameters.

Smaller changes

  • countreg() uses bootstrap standard errors when bootstraps is given without stderr, as the other estimators do.
  • countreg_alloc(): an offset in alloc_formula or threshold_formula is an error (it was dropped); alloc_formula = ~ 0 + f with an ordered link is coded with contrasts; predict(random = "posterior") without random parameters is an error instead of a marginal prediction.
  • Moments of user-defined families without a variance function no longer take minutes for PMFs that do not sum to exactly 1.
  • Documentation: countreg_fe() clustered standard errors equal fixest’s when vcov = ~ group is given (fixest 0.13 defaults to iid); the shared error message of the mixtures lists rpar; mixture history/posterior conditioning updates only the class probabilities.

Total-plus-allocation models

  • New countreg_alloc() fits a total count jointly with its allocation across categories, such as crashes by severity: the total follows any count family (with distribution-parameter formulas), and the split follows an ordered probit or ordered logit model for ordered categories (such as severity), with generalized thresholds (threshold_formula), or a multinomial logit model (link = "mnl") for unordered categories (such as crash types), with category-specific coefficients. The default multinomial likelihood is a proper joint likelihood of the category counts (likelihood-ratio tests, AIC and BIC are valid); with a Poisson total the categories are independent Poissons, and with an NB2 total and no covariates the fit equals negmultinom(). likelihood = "fractional" gives the share-weighted quasi-likelihood of Shabab et al. (2026, AMAR 51:100440), with sandwich standard errors and no AIC. Zero totals are part of the model (they contribute P(c = 0) and nothing about the split); truncated = TRUE fits a zero-truncated total for data that hold only units with at least one event, and a message points to it when the data have no zero totals. predict() gives the expected counts by category, the probabilities, the total, and the expected total or counts given at least one event; simulate(), summary(), tidy(), glance() and confint() work, and tv() can be used in every formula. Analytic gradients for all parts.
  • countreg_alloc() has random parameters in each equation: rpar_total, rpar_alloc (the propensity) and rpar_threshold (a common random term in the gaps between thresholds) add normal random deviations to the coefficients, drawn once per unit of group_var and shared by its rows (the years of a site), with correlation = "none", "within" (each equation) or "across" (between the total and the allocation). The likelihood is simulated with randomly shifted Halton draws (rpar_draws, a stored seed) and has analytic gradients through the draws’ posterior weights. Checked against exact Gauss-Hermite quadrature (within 0.05 of the log-likelihood with 500 draws) and by recovering correlated random intercepts. predict() gives marginal predictions and, with random = "posterior", Empirical Bayes predictions for units in the estimation data; simulate() draws new coefficients for each unit; summary() shows the standard deviations and correlations.
  • countreg_alloc() has a shared site-year term (shared_formula): one standard normal draw per row that enters the total, the propensity and/or the threshold gaps (shared_in) with covariate-dependent loadings, so a row’s total and its split share an unobserved factor (the term eta of Shabab et al. 2026, with a loading for each equation, which allows a negative correlation too). It is integrated by adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature (shared_nodes, centred and scaled for each row; the fit warns if twice the nodes change the log-likelihood) inside the draws of the unit-level random parameters, with analytic gradients. With truncated = TRUE each row’s likelihood is divided by its marginal probability of a positive total. A Poisson total with the term only in the total reproduces the Poisson-lognormal (PLN) fit.
  • New vignette “Total-plus-allocation models: counts by severity”.

Multivariate count models

  • New countreg_mv() fits several count outcomes observed on the same units (crashes by severity or type at each site), each with its own count family, mean formula and distribution-parameter formulas (family = c(pdo = "NB2", injury = "PIG"), formulas given as cbind(y1, y2) ~ x or a list of formulas, one per outcome). In this first version the equations are independent given the covariates, so the fit equals separate countreg() fits; one fit gives joint predictions, probabilities, simulations, and Wald tests across equations. Analytic gradients, a Newton polish after BFGS, and normal, robust or cluster-robust standard errors. New vignette “Multivariate count models”.
  • countreg_mv() has random parameters in each equation (rpar_formula, one formula for every outcome or one per outcome), drawn per unit of group_var and correlated across equations (correlation = "across", the default, "within" or "none"). Poisson outcomes with correlated normal random intercepts give the multivariate Poisson-lognormal model (MVPLN); any family can be used in each equation. Simulated likelihood with analytic gradients, checked against numerical derivatives, exact two-dimensional Gauss-Hermite quadrature and recovery of correlated intercepts. predict() gives joint (type = "joint") and conditional (type = "conditional") probabilities of the outcomes, and Empirical Bayes predictions (random = "posterior"); simulate() draws new random parameters for each unit; summary() shows the standard deviations and correlations.
  • countreg_mv() has copulas (copula = "gaussian" for two outcomes, "frank", "clayton" or "gumbel" for any number) that join the outcomes’ own distributions. The likelihood is the exact probability of the observed counts (the copula’s volume over the rectangle of each count, summed over the 2^J corners), not a midpoint or jittered approximation, and all parameters are estimated together, started from the separate equations (inference functions for margins). The Gaussian copula uses an exact bivariate normal distribution function (the algorithm of Genz, accurate to about 1e-15). summary() reports the copula parameter and its Kendall’s tau, predict() gives joint and conditional probabilities from the copula, and simulate() draws from it. Checked against numerical integration, the probabilities’ sums and margins, independence limits, and recovery of the dependence of every family.
  • Copula models of countreg_mv() have analytic gradients (the derivatives of the copula and of each outcome’s distribution function), and copulas can be combined with random parameters (copula with rpar_formula): given a unit’s random parameters, the outcomes of each row are joined by the copula, so the random parameters carry the dependence between units over time and the copula the dependence within each row. Joint and conditional probabilities and simulations integrate over the random parameters.
  • Random-parameter standard deviations (the diagonal of the Cholesky factor) of countreg_alloc() and countreg_mv() are reported as positive. In countreg_alloc() the intercept is random only when a random-parameter formula has the term 1 itself (~ 1, ~ 1 + x), as in the mixtures; ~ x makes only the slope random.

Random parameters within latent classes

  • countreg_mix() and countreg_lc() have random parameters within the components (classes), a latent-class random-parameters model: rpar_formula makes the coefficients of some variables vary from unit to unit (panel, or row) around their class means, with class-specific scales (Component<k>:SD:) or scales shared by all classes (shared = list(rpar = TRUE)), any of the distributions of countreg_rp() (rpardists) or correlated normal parameters (correlated = TRUE), and rpar_draws simulation draws per unit (the same draws for every class, from a seed derived from seed). Each class’s simulated likelihood is that of countreg_rp(), with analytic gradients for the direct maximization and the EM steps (at most 25 EM iterations per start, since EM converges slowly here). Predictions, count probabilities, class probabilities (prior, posterior and history), residuals, rootogram() and margEffTable() integrate over the random parameters, and simulate() draws new coefficients for every unit. Checked against numerical derivatives, against exact Gauss-Hermite quadrature, and by recovering two classes with different random slopes.

Time-varying effects (temporal instability)

  • New formula term tv(x, time = year) gives x one effect per period, in the formulas of every estimator: the mean, the distribution parameters, zero and underreporting models, countreg_rp()’s rpar_formula, and the fixed parts of countreg_hier(), countreg_fe(), countreg_mix() and the random-effects models. tv(1, time = year) gives a time-varying intercept. Four bases: "step" (default; the first period’s effect and the change at each later period, so a zero coefficient means equal effects in adjacent periods), "level" (one effect per period), "hinge" (the cumulative “spline indicators” of Shabab et al. 2026, AMAR 51:100440, where a zero coefficient continues the earlier trend instead of keeping the effect equal) and "smooth" (the varying-coefficient smooth s(time, by = x)). The step, level and hinge bases give the same fit. The periods are stored for prediction; a period not in the estimation data is an error, or uses the nearest period with new_time = "nearest".
  • New temporal_effects() gives each period’s effect with its standard error (A V A’) and confidence interval, and temporal_tests() gives Wald tests that the effects are equal in all periods and of each change between adjacent periods. Both work for every basis, give the same results for the step, level and hinge bases, and accept a robust vcov.
  • margEffTable() does not treat the time variable of a tv() term as a predictor.
  • New vignette “Time-varying effects: temporal instability”.

Sampling weights

  • countreg() and countreg_rp() gain weight_type = c("frequency", "sampling"). Frequency weights (the default) count each row as that many independent observations, as before. Sampling (survey or inverse-probability) weights make the weighted log-likelihood a pseudo-likelihood: standard errors default to the robust sandwich with meat sum((w s)(w s)’) and a G / (G - 1) factor, so they do not change when all weights are rescaled (with frequency weights, multiplying every weight by 100 shrinks them 10-fold); the number of units is the number of rows or panels; the bootstrap is refused; summary() notes that LR tests, AIC and BIC are not valid; and regCompTest() runs no LR test.

Faster random-parameter estimation

  • countreg_rp() now gives the optimizer the analytic gradient of the simulated log-likelihood instead of a numeric one. Each panel’s score is the posterior-weighted average over draws of the family’s score in the log mean times the derivative of the log mean in each parameter. This covers fixed coefficients; normal, lognormal, uniform, triangular and gamma random parameters; correlated (Cholesky) parameters; heterogeneity in means and in variances; and distribution-parameter formulas. Poisson, NB1, NB2 and NBP have closed-form scores. The other families use central differences in the log mean and in each distribution parameter, which take two density evaluations per distribution parameter whatever the number of regression parameters. On washington_roads with three random parameters (9 parameters), a 500-draw NB2 fit by BFGS takes 8.6 s instead of 41 s, and a 100-draw fit by BHHH takes 6 s instead of 38 s, with the same log-likelihood. Newton-Raphson’s Hessian is now the numeric derivative of the analytic gradient, which is faster and more accurate than second differences of the log-likelihood. options(flexCountReg.rp_gradient = "numeric") restores the numeric gradient.
  • countreg_rp() no longer reports convergence where the optimizer only stopped because the log-likelihood changed little between iterations. BHHH, NR and BFGSR stop on that test, and a crawling BHHH also meets it far from the maximum. On washington_roads, a 100-draw NB2 fit with three random parameters started from the matching countreg() fit “converged” at -1086.9, 21.6 below the maximum. The fit now checks the Newton decrement g’(-H)^-1 g at the estimates, which is twice the gain a Newton step predicts. Above 0.1 it sets converged = FALSE and warns with the predicted gain. Fits with max.iters = 0 by BFGS, which optim() reported as converged, are flagged the same way. The decrement is stored as model$newton_decrement.
  • Families can declare a score function in the internal registry; the NB1, NB2 and NBP scores are shared by countreg() and countreg_rp().

Generalized additive count models (smooth terms)

  • countreg() and countreg_rp() accept the penalized smooth terms of the mgcv package (s(), te(), ti(), t2()) in their formulas:
    • In countreg(): the mean, the distribution-parameter formulas, the zero model and the underreporting model.
    • In countreg_rp(): the fixed part of the mean, het_mean_formula, het_var_formula and the distribution-parameter formulas.
    • Smooth bases are built once on the estimation rows and rebuilt for new data with the same knots.
  • Fitting is by penalized maximum likelihood, finished with Newton steps on the penalized Hessian so that weakly penalized smooths reach the optimum. The smoothing parameters are selected by generalized Fellner-Schall updates (Wood and Fasiolo 2017), or fixed with the new argument sp.
  • Standard errors are Bayesian, (H + S_lambda)^-1, by default; robust and cluster-robust versions are available.
  • summary() reports each smooth by its effective degrees of freedom, with an approximate test (Wood 2013), instead of its basis coefficients. logLik() counts the total effective degrees of freedom, so AIC() compares smooth and parametric models.
  • Agreement with mgcv:
    • With fixed smoothing parameters, the estimates, log-likelihood, effective degrees of freedom and standard errors equal those of mgcv::gam() for Poisson and NB2 (with the dispersion fixed).
    • The selected smoothing parameters were within about 5% of mgcv’s REML choice in the tests.
  • New smooth_estimates() and plot_smooths() evaluate and plot each smooth with pointwise and simultaneous confidence bands. Their values equal mgcv’s term predictions.
  • The random-effects panel models renb(), repois(), poislind_re() and negmultinom() also accept smooth terms, in the mean and, for negmultinom(), in the panel-level dispersion formulas. They have the same penalized fitting, sp argument and Bayesian standard errors. negmultinom() with family NM2 and repois() are the same model, and give the same smooth.
  • repois() gains an analytic score for its penalized fits, which made a smooth fit about 10 times faster (46 s to 4 s on washington_roads).
  • countreg_fe() accepts smooth terms of variables that change within groups, with all three of its estimators. A smooth of a variable that is constant within groups is absorbed by the fixed effects and gives an error.
    • The multi-dimension Poisson estimator uses penalized IRLS.
    • The bases are built on the rows used in estimation, after the all-zero and single-observation groups are dropped.
    • With the same smoothing parameters, the estimates equal mgcv::gam() with group dummies: to 1e-8 for one dimension, 1e-14 for two, and 1e-5 for NB2 with the dispersion fixed.
  • countreg_mix() and countreg_lc() accept smooth terms in the mean, the distribution-parameter formulas and the mixing (membership) formula.
    • Each component’s copy of a smooth, and each membership logit’s, has its own smoothing parameter.
    • The multi-start search is unpenalized; the selected, label-aligned solution is then refitted by penalized likelihood.
    • One component reproduces countreg() exactly.
    • In a simulated two-component Poisson mixture (a sine-shaped and a linear component), the smooths recovered both shapes: a correlation of 1.000 with the sine, and a slope of 0.296 for a true 0.3. The class shares were 0.386 and 0.614, for true 0.4 and 0.6.
    • Every estimator of the package now accepts smooth terms.
  • All mgcv smooth classes can be used, among them by smooths (factor by gives a curve per level; numeric by gives a varying coefficient), random-effect (bs = "re"), factor-smooth (bs = "fs") and Markov random field (bs = "mrf", with xt = list(nb = nb)) smooths. With fixed smoothing parameters they reproduce mgcv::gam().
    • Objects in a smooth’s arguments, such as the neighborhood list, are taken from the formula’s environment, not from the data.
    • smooth_estimates() and plot_smooths() show every smooth type: curves per level, factor effects with intervals, and the coefficient of a numeric by.
  • New diagnostics for smooth terms:
    • smooth_check(): a basis-dimension check (a k-index with a permutation p-value) computed from randomized quantile residuals.
    • concurvity_fcr(): the share of each smooth that the other terms can reproduce, observed and worst case.
    • smooth_derivatives() and plot_derivatives(): derivatives with pointwise and simultaneous bands.
    • plot_surface(): two-variable smooths, masked away from the data.
    • calibration_by(): observed and predicted means, probabilities of zero and variances by quantile groups of a covariate.
  • New vignette, “Smooth effects: generalized additive count models” (vignette("smooth-effects")).
  • Bootstrap standard errors are not yet available with smooth terms.

Hierarchical count models

  • New countreg_hier() fits count models with normally distributed random effects at any number of grouping levels, nested or crossed, written as in lme4: (1 | site), (1 + lnaadt | county) (correlated intercepts and slopes), (lnaadt || county) (uncorrelated), (1 | county/segment) (nested) and (1 | site) + (1 | year) (crossed). Every count family can be used, including user-defined ones, with distribution-parameter formulas, offsets and frequency weights.
  • Two integration engines: adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature for one grouping term (9 points per effect by default), and the Laplace approximation with sparse matrices for any number of terms. engine = "auto" chooses between them. Each covariance matrix is estimated through its Cholesky factor with an unconstrained diagonal, so a variance can be estimated as zero; such singular fits are reported, and the Wald standard errors of that term’s variance components are not. The derivatives of the log-density are analytic for the Poisson, NB1 and NB2 families and numerical for the others.
  • Estimates, log-likelihoods and standard errors equal those of lme4::glmer() (Poisson, Laplace and quadrature) and glmmTMB (Poisson, NB1 and NB2; random intercepts and slopes, crossed and nested effects), with log-likelihood differences of 1e-6 or less.
  • Methods: summary(), predict() with re.form (condition on all, some or none of the levels), allow.new.levels and marginal (integrate the remaining effects out of the mean, exp(eta + z’ Sigma z / 2)), fitted(), residuals(), simulate() (with the groups’ effects or new ones), fixef(), ranef() (conditional modes with posterior variances), VarCorr(), tidy() and glance(). fixef(), ranef() and VarCorr() are the nlme generics, so they work alongside lme4.
  • margEffTable() works with countreg_hier() (the grouping variables are not candidates, and delta-method standard errors account for the fixed coefficients) and leaves out the regressors a fixed-effects model removed as not identified.
  • New re_lrtest(): likelihood-ratio test of a random-effect term, with the boundary-corrected (chi-bar-squared) p-value.
  • New vignette, “Hierarchical count models” (vignette("hierarchical-count-models")).
  • Smooth terms s() and t2() in the fixed part, fitted in their mixed-model form (as in gamm4): the penalized part of each smooth is a block of normal coefficients with variance 1 / lambda, so the smoothing parameters are estimated by the marginal likelihood with the variance components. Smoothing parameters, EDF and curves equal those of mgcv::gam(method = "ML") with bs = "re" group effects. A formula with smooths and no grouping term is a GAM fitted by marginal likelihood.
  • re_dist = "uniform", "triangular" or "gamma" (one grouping term) gives non-normal random effects, fitted by maximum simulated likelihood (engine = "msl", re_draws randomly shifted Halton draws per group). With "gamma" the multiplicative group effect is gamma with mean 1; a Poisson model with gamma effects reproduces repois().
  • predict(history = ) estimates the effects of the groups from a separate set of past counts, so a forecast never uses its own outcomes.
  • confint(method = "profile") gives profile-likelihood intervals for the random-effect standard deviations (and fixed coefficients); they equal glmmTMB’s.
  • cre and cre_group add the group means of time-varying covariates (correlated random effects), tested with cre_test().
  • Not yet available in countreg_hier(): non-normal random effects at more than one level, smooth terms in the distribution-parameter formulas, and te()/ti() smooths (use t2()).

Fixed-effects count models

  • New countreg_fe() estimates count models with fixed effects for one or more grouping variables (fixef = ~ site or ~ site + year). It chooses among three estimators:
    • Poisson with one dimension: the conditional likelihood.
    • Poisson with several dimensions: IRLS with alternating projections, as in fixest::fepois().
    • Any other family, including families from new_count_family(), with one dimension: the dummy-variable likelihood with the group intercepts concentrated out.
  • Groups with all-zero counts or a single observation are dropped and reported, and regressors without variation within groups are removed with a warning.
  • Standard errors are cluster-robust by the first fixed-effect variable by default. The log-likelihood is that of the dummy-variable model, with degrees of freedom that count the fixed effects.
  • jackknife = TRUE applies the split-panel jackknife of Dhaene and Jochmans (2015). In simulations with 200 units it removed most of the NB2 dispersion bias with 5 or 10 periods, but did not improve the slopes, and it is unreliable below 4 periods, where a warning is given.
  • predict() uses each known group’s effect. Groups not in the estimation data give NA unless newgroup = "mean_fe".
  • Estimates, log-likelihoods and dropped groups equal those of fixest::fepois() (one and two ways) and fixest::fenegbin(). The cluster-robust standard errors equal fixest’s with ssc(adj = FALSE).
  • countreg_rp(), renb() and repois() gain cre = ~ x1 + x2 for correlated random effects (Mundlak 1978). The units’ means of the listed time-varying regressors are added to the mean model, computed on the estimation rows and stored with the fit. Predictions for known units use their training means; new units use the means of their own rows.
  • New cre_test(), a Wald test that the coefficients of those means are zero: a robust test of random against fixed effects. In simulations with unit effects correlated with the regressor, the plain random-effects slope was biased (0.63 for a true 0.5), the slope with cre was 0.505, equal to fixed effects, and the test rejected in every replication. With uncorrelated effects, it rejected in 7% of replications at the 5% level.
  • New vignette, “Fixed-effects count models” (vignette("fixed-effects-count-models")), with a section on correlated random effects.

Cluster-robust standard errors and the sandwich package

  • countreg() and countreg_rp() gain stderr = "cluster" with cluster = ~ corridor (or column names, or a vector of ids). Two or more variables (~ corridor + year) give multiway clustering (Cameron, Gelbach and Miller 2011). The scores of the independent units (rows, or panels) are summed within clusters, with the factor G / (G - 1). Clusters may be coarser than the panels (sites within corridors) but may not split a panel. Giving cluster alone selects cluster-robust standard errors. With frequency weights, a row’s copies are in its cluster. summary() reports the number of clusters.
  • vcov() gains type = c("fit", "hessian", "robust", "cluster") and cluster, which recompute the covariance matrix from the stored scores without refitting. This works for countreg(), countreg_rp(), renb(), repois() and poislind_re() fits. With keep_data = FALSE, the clusters are given as a vector.
  • New estfun() and bread() methods for the sandwich package, so sandwich::vcovCL(), vcovHC(), sandwich(), lmtest::coeftest() and tools built on them work with flexCountReg fits. One-way and two-way cluster covariances equal sandwich::vcovCL(type = "HC0") to 1e-10.

User-defined count distributions

  • New new_count_family() and count_param() define a count distribution from its log PMF, with up to two parameters, each with a log, logit or identity link. The family object can be passed as family to countreg(), countreg_rp(), countreg_mix() and countreg_lc(). It works with distribution-parameter formulas, zero-inflated and hurdle models, predictions, quantile residuals, rootograms, simulate() and robust or cluster-robust standard errors.
    • Optional mean, variance, cdf, rand and valid functions can be given. Without them, the moments and the CDF come from summing the PMF, and random draws from inverting the CDF.
    • A user NB2 reproduces the built-in NB2 in fixed, random-parameter, hurdle and mixture fits. A user zero-inflated NB2 reproduces zero_formula = ~ 1.
    • Each family is registered under its name and a hash of its definition, so two families with the same name do not collide.
    • The fit stores the family, so a model saved with saveRDS() works in a new R session.
    • Underreporting is not available for user families.
  • New check_count_family() checks a family over a grid of means and parameter values. It tests that the PMF sums to one, that mean, variance, cdf and rand agree with the PMF, that the function is vectorized, and that missing or invalid values cause no errors.
  • New vignette, “Fitting your own count distribution” (vignette("user-defined-count-distributions")), with a one-inflated negative binomial as the worked example.

Interactive app

  • New launch_app() opens an interactive interface to flexCountReg in a web browser, with a tab for each step: load a bundled example or a CSV file and create new variables (logs, powers, standardized values, indicators, products, ratios, categories, factors); specify and estimate count regression, random-parameter, random-effects panel (RENB, Poisson-Lindley, Poisson, negative multinomial), finite-mixture and latent-class models (any family, exposure or log offset, frequency weights, distribution-parameter, membership and shared terms, panels); inspect the summary, coefficients, numerical checks, class sizes and starts; diagnose fits (rootogram, randomized quantile residuals, CURE plot); compare them (with the reasons when they are not comparable); predict for an editable table of scenarios or for uploaded new data, with confidence, prediction and tolerance intervals for count regressions; and download the analysis. The Diagnose and Predict tabs work on any completed model (a selector, which moves to each new fit), plots can be saved as JPEG files at a chosen size and resolution, and new data get the variables created on the Data tab that the model needs, with the means, standard deviations and categories of the training data.
  • Everything the app runs (data loading, new variables, fits, diagnostics, predictions, intervals and comparisons) is compiled into R code that calls the package’s functions, evaluated from that code and appended to a session script, shown in the app and downloaded as analysis.R; the script reproduces the whole session without the app (the download also holds the settings of each fit as JSON and a manifest with versions and warnings). Column names and typed values enter the code only as names, numbers or strings, never as code. An action that fails reports its error and leaves the session running.
  • Models are estimated in background R processes (callr), so the interface stays responsive and fits can be canceled; a slow earlier fit never replaces a newer one. Predictions and intervals also run in the background: an interval for a model whose covariance matrix is not positive definite uses a parametric bootstrap (200 refits), which can take many minutes, and the app says so when it starts and offers to cancel it. Data, fits and jobs belong to one browser session.
  • Models built in the app can include interactions between pairs of predictors (entered as a:b; main effects stay in the model), and the Fit page has a Marginal effects tab running margEffTable() (average marginal effects or elasticities; pseudo-elasticities or discrete changes for indicators; delta-method or bootstrap standard errors) in the background, with the code added to the session script and the table downloadable as CSV.
  • Exports are reproducible: each uploaded file is stored at its own path (data/data_1.csv, data/newdata_1.csv, …) with its MD5 checksum in the manifest; warnings and messages of every result are shown beside it and listed in the manifest with the uncertainty method, accepted bootstrap refits and seed; and stochastic requests (bootstrap intervals, tolerance intervals, bootstrap marginal effects) fix their seed when they are made, so the exported script replays them exactly.
  • The app runs the models added in this release: hierarchical models (countreg_hier(): a grouping column, random slopes, correlated or uncorrelated, a second level crossed with or nested in the first, and normal, gamma, uniform or triangular effects) and fixed-effects models (countreg_fe(): one or two dimensions, the split-panel jackknife, cluster-robust standard errors by default). Any model can have smooth (nonlinear) effects s(x) of numeric predictors, shown on the Diagnose page (“Smooth effects”, plot_smooths()); random-parameter, hierarchical and random-effects models can add group means of predictors (correlated random effects, cre); count regression and random-parameter models offer cluster-robust standard errors (with a cluster column) and sampling weights. Predictions for hierarchical and fixed-effects models take the group of each scenario, and settings files from earlier versions of the app still load.
  • The app’s packages (shiny, bslib, DT, callr, jsonlite, zip) are suggested, not imported: the statistical functions do not need them, and launch_app() offers to install any that are missing. app_object() returns the app for deployment or testing.

Finite mixtures and latent classes

  • New countreg_mix() estimates finite mixtures of count distributions and finite-mixture count regressions; countreg_lc() is the same model under the latent-class vocabulary (classes, membership_formula). Both normalize their arguments into one specification and call one engine, so equivalent calls give identical fits. Supported specifications:
    • distribution-only mixtures (y ~ 1), including fits to exact-count frequency tables through weights;
    • mixture regressions with component-specific coefficients, or with whole terms shared by all components (shared = list(mean = "x")) and shared distribution-parameter blocks (shared = list(dis1 = TRUE));
    • constant mixing proportions, covariate-dependent membership probabilities (a multinomial logit, mixing_formula = ~ z, last component as reference), or known fixed proportions (fixed_mixing), which add no parameters;
    • any count family of countreg() in the components, the same in all of them or different ones (e.g. family = c(base = "POISSON", tail = "NB2")), with distribution-parameter formulas;
    • panel mixtures (group_var): one class per panel, with the class probability entering once per panel (product of the rows’ probabilities before the sum over classes);
    • offsets and frequency weights (outside the logarithm of the mixture; constant within panels).
  • Estimation uses several reproducible starts (n_starts, seed), EM iterations with weighted M-steps (analytic scores for Poisson, NB1 and NB2 components), and direct maximization of the observed-data log-likelihood to polish the best solutions (mixture_control(), lc_control()). Every start is recorded (fit$model$starts), including whether several starts reached the selected solution. Components of the same family are numbered by increasing average expected count.
  • Standard errors come from the observed information of the full parameter vector (stderr = "normal"), unit-level sandwich scores ("robust"), or a bootstrap of independent units that refits the full mixture with several starts and aligns component labels within families ("boot"). The fit records the gradient, the definiteness and conditioning of the observed information, and ambiguous bootstrap label matches.
  • Methods: summary() (coefficients grouped by component, shared parameters and mixing model; prior and posterior class sizes; entropy, relative entropy and ICL; start stability; numerical checks), print(), coef(), vcov(), logLik() (free parameters only, independent units for BIC), predict() with explicit targets (type = "response", "component", "variance", "prob", "link"; conditioning = "prior", "history" for panel forecasts from earlier outcomes only, or the retrospective "posterior"), fitted(), residuals() (response, Pearson with the full mixture variance, and randomized quantile residuals from the mixture distribution function), simulate() (one class per row or panel), tidy(), glance() and augment(). New component_probs() / class_probs() return prior, history-conditioned or posterior class probabilities.
  • rootogram() and cureplot() accept mixture models (prior mixture probabilities and means), and margEffTable() includes variables that enter only the membership model (delta-method standard errors with the full covariance matrix).
  • Not available yet, with explanatory errors: confidence, prediction and tolerance intervals for mixture predictions; bootstrap standard errors of marginal effects; likelihood-ratio tests involving mixtures (regCompTest() refuses them, because the chi-square reference distribution does not hold when the number of components changes). Zero-inflated, hurdle and underreporting components inside mixtures and component-specific formulas are not implemented. Mixtures of families other than Poisson, NB1 and NB2 are labeled experimental: their component distributions are those of countreg() (one-component fits agree with it), but recovery of such mixtures has not been studied.
  • New vignettes: “Finite mixtures of count distributions” and “Latent-class and finite-mixture count regression”, and a recovery and coverage study, inst/validation/finite-mixtures/ (its CORES setting runs the replicates in parallel with the same results). In 200 replicates of each of seven designs (well and weakly separated Poisson mixtures, a latent-class NB2 regression with membership covariates and a shared dispersion, a panel latent-class model, and a Poisson + NB2 mixture), every fit converged; Wald intervals covered 0.89 to 0.985 (Monte Carlo standard errors about 0.015), and the label-invariant mixture mean was nearly unbiased in every design. With weakly separated components and n = 300 the low component’s intercept was biased (-0.18) and its standard errors unstable, and 40% of the fits were reached by only one of five starts: use more starts and treat component-specific inference with caution in such data.
  • A warning (and a note in summary()) flags components of the same family with nearly identical parameters: the fit is then effectively one component fewer and its shares are arbitrary.

New count distributions

  • Eight new count distributions, each with density, distribution, quantile and random-generation functions following base R conventions (recycling, NA/NaN, NaN with a warning for invalid parameters, lower.tail, log/log.p):
    • discrete Weibull (ddweib(), pdweib(), qdweib(), rdweib());
    • double Poisson, exactly normalized (ddpo(), …);
    • Delaporte in a mean parameterization (ddelaporte(), …);
    • generalized Hermite of order m (dghermite(), …);
    • hyper-Poisson (dhpois(), …);
    • gamma renewal count (dgcount(), …);
    • Polya-Aeppli, the Poisson-Tweedie distribution with power 1.5 (dpaeppli(), …).
  • Probabilities are computed on the log scale, and upper tails (lower.tail = FALSE) are computed directly rather than as one minus the distribution function, so tiny tail probabilities keep their relative accuracy. Quantiles are the smallest count whose distribution function reaches the requested probability.
  • Negative binomial-generalized exponential mixture (dnbge(), pnbge(), qnbge(), rnbge()): NB2 with a mean-one generalized exponential random effect, computed by the adaptive quadrature used for PGE.

New regression families

  • countreg() and countreg_rp() gain the families "DW", "DPO", "DELAPORTE", "HERMITE" (order 2), "HERMITE3", "HERMITE4", "HYPERPOIS", "GAMMACOUNT", "PA" (Poisson-Tweedie with power 1.5) and "NBGE". All are parameterized by the mean, so coefficients are effects on the expected count. For DW, DPO, HYPERPOIS and GAMMACOUNT, whose means have no closed form, the natural parameter of each observation is found by solving the mean equation in compiled code; these families are slower to fit and have a numerical domain (shape in [1e-6, 1e6], mean up to 1e9).
  • Shares in [0, 1] (Delaporte and Hermite rho) use a logit link, labeled logit(rho).
  • Prediction, Pearson and quantile residuals, simulation, rootograms and summaries work for all new families. Likelihood-ratio tests against Poisson are reported for DPO, HYPERPOIS and GAMMACOUNT (interior restriction). Underreporting (binomial thinning) is available for DELAPORTE, NBGE, HERMITE and PA.
  • countreg_rp() uses family-specific starting values for the distribution parameters when the registry provides them (the new families start at their Poisson or geometric limit rather than at log-scale -2).

Confidence, prediction and tolerance intervals

  • predict() gains interval = "confidence" (for the expected count) and interval = "prediction" (for one new count), with level, for countreg() models. Estimation uncertainty is represented by parameter vectors from the asymptotic normal distribution of the estimates, evaluated at deterministic Halton points (reproducible), or by a parametric bootstrap (uncertainty = "bootstrap"), which is also used when the covariance matrix is not positive definite. Prediction intervals are integer quantiles of the predictive distribution (the count PMF averaged over the parameter vectors).
  • New tolerance_interval(): content tolerance intervals (content and confidence levels; two-sided, upper or lower; pointwise or simultaneous) for countreg() models. The default joint method returns the narrowest integer interval whose content is at least the requested fraction at every evaluated point of the confidence set; the envelope method uses per-tail worst cases; intercept-only Poisson models use the exact common-rate construction. Zero-inflated, hurdle and underreporting components are included. A reproducible coverage study is in inst/validation/intervals/.

Starting values for the dispersion

  • countreg() now starts the dispersion parameter of NB1, NB2, PIG1, PIG2 and PIG at a moment estimate from the Poisson starting fit (the auxiliary regression of Cameron and Trivedi) instead of alpha = 1. With the old start, quasi-Newton optimizers could step onto the flat region alpha -> 0 and stop there with a falsely “converged” Poisson fit: NB2 with method = "BFGS" gave log-likelihood -228.48 instead of -195.56 on warpbreaks, and -182.29 instead of -180.11 on InsectSprays. Results now match MASS::glm.nb(). Fits that already reached the maximum are unchanged.

Standard errors at flat likelihood directions

  • When the Hessian is singular, standard errors still use a generalized inverse, but parameters involved in a direction where the likelihood is flat now get NA variances and standard errors instead of zero (a zero standard error read as perfect precision, e.g. the random-effect parameter of a Poisson-Lindley random-effects model at its boundary). The warning names those parameters.
  • When the Hessian is invertible but not negative definite (for example an NB2 dispersion drifting toward zero on Poisson-like data), the negative variances already gave NA standard errors; a warning now names those parameters instead of leaving them silently NA.

Vignettes

  • Seventeen vignettes, grouped on the package website as Start here, Diagnose and interpret, Model structure, Finite mixtures and latent classes, Predict and validate, and Advanced. New (besides the two finite-mixture vignettes above): getting started; data, exposure and weights; diagnosing count models; predictions, marginal effects and elasticities; modeling distribution parameters; zeros, hurdles and sampling; underreporting and identification; predictive validation; prediction for panel data; numerical reliability; simulation studies; and adding a count distribution (for contributors). The three earlier vignettes are revised.

  • inst/validation/simulation-studies/count-regression-study.R is a parameterized simulation study (Poisson, NB2 and a negative multinomial panel) with one random-number stream per replicate; its summary and settings are saved alongside it. The per-replicate results of this study and of the interval coverage study are kept in the source repository but left out of the package build. ## New data

  • abalone_rings: shell-ring counts and measurements of 4,177 abalone from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (CC BY 4.0), a non-transportation example with conditionally underdispersed counts. The preparation script and source hashes are in data-raw/ of the source repository; data terms are in the installed DATA-LICENSES.md.

  • stream_salamanders: repeated counts of seven stream salamander groups at 23 sites (Price et al., 2016; Dryad, CC0), prepared from the original deposit. Zero-heavy, overdispersed and grouped by site.

tidymodels and broom

  • tidy(), glance() and augment() methods, using the generics package (re-exported, so library(flexCountReg) provides them). tidy() returns the standard broom columns plus a component column (mean, distribution, underreporting, random-parameter and heterogeneity parameters), with conf.int and exponentiate (incidence rate ratios for the mean model). tidy() now works for every estimator. broom is no longer a dependency.
  • New count_reg() parsnip model with a "flexCountReg" engine, registered when parsnip is loaded (parsnip is suggested, not required). The count family is a main argument and can be tuned with count_family() (a dials parameter). Case weights are passed as frequency weights.
  • predict() accepts new_data (the tidymodels name) as well as newdata.
  • Standard errors are NA (instead of 0) when the estimated variance is negative, which happens for weakly identified parameters. regCompTable() shows such standard errors as NA without significance stars.

Breaking changes and changed results

  • summary() now returns a summary.flexCountReg object with a print method (coefficients with z statistics, the standard-error type, log-likelihood, AIC, BIC, N and panels, convergence, and a likelihood-ratio test against Poisson for countreg() models). Use summary(m)$coefficients for the coefficient matrix, or tibble::as_tibble(summary(m)) for the tibble that summary() returned before. The offset is shown as a note, not as a coefficient row.
  • countreg() and countreg_rp() compute the final Hessian, and so every Hessian-based, robust and cluster-robust standard error, adaptively. maxLik’s default step is 1e-6, where rounding error is about 0.2 per Hessian entry for a log-likelihood near 1000. That made the standard errors of weakly determined parameters wrong. In the README’s generalized NBP model on washington_roads they were up to 25% too large (ln(p): 0.229, now 0.183).
    • The Hessian is computed at steps h and h/2 (h = 1e-3 times the size of each estimate) and combined by Richardson extrapolation. Larger steps (for log-likelihoods computed with quadrature, series or Bessel functions) and smaller ones are tried when the two disagree.
    • Families with an analytic gradient (Poisson, NB1, NB2, and countreg_rp() in general) difference the gradient; the others use second differences of the log-likelihood.
    • The fit stores model$hessian_accuracy, the largest relative change of a standard error between the two steps, and warns when it exceeds 1%.
    • Checked against independent Hessians, the standard errors agree to about 6e-5 or better for the Poisson, NB1, NB2, NBP, PIG, PIG1, PLN, GP1 and DW families. The Sichel family agrees to 0.15%, for its weakly identified gamma.
    • BHHH fits keep the outer-product Hessian of the scores.
  • Hessian-based, robust and cluster-robust covariances use the symmetric part of the numeric Hessian. In poorly conditioned fits the inverse amplified the Hessian’s small asymmetry. For example, a renb() fit by Nelder-Mead on washington_roads had a negative robust variance for ln(a-1); it is now 0.036. In well-conditioned fits the change is negligible.
  • countreg_rp() gives each unit (panel, or row without group_var) its own simulation draws by default: new argument draws = c("per_unit", "shared"). Unit u uses draws (u - 1) R + 1 to u R of one Halton sequence, after its first 10 points (Train 2009, Sec. 9.3.3). With shared draws, as before, draw r is the same for every panel, so simulation errors are correlated across panels and do not average out as panels are added. On washington_roads (NB2, random speed50 and lnlength, 12 scrambling seeds), per-unit draws cut the error of the random-parameter means and standard deviations by a factor of 2 to 5 at 50 and 200 draws. The intercept and the log-likelihood varied more across seeds than with shared draws. Empirical Bayes predictions regenerate each estimation panel’s own draws (by panel id), and new panels get new draws. draws = "shared" reproduces earlier fits.
  • Scrambled Halton draws (scrambled = TRUE in countreg_rp(), and in interval simulations) now depend on their seed. randtoolbox scrambles with its own generator, which set.seed() does not reach. So every “scrambled” fit used the same scrambling (randtoolbox’s default, seed 0), whatever the stored draw_seed, and different seeds gave identical results. Fits made before this change still predict with the draws they were estimated with.
  • countreg_rp(scrambled = TRUE) now randomizes the Halton draws with a random shift (Cranley-Patterson rotation): each unit’s block of plain Halton points is shifted by its own uniform amount per dimension, modulo 1, with the shifts generated from the fit’s draw_seed. It used randtoolbox’s scrambled (“mixed”) Halton sequence, whose consecutive per-unit blocks biased the simulated log-likelihood, and more draws did not remove the bias. For a Poisson random intercept on washington_roads (exact maximum -1069.365 by adaptive quadrature), scrambled fits gave -1069.406 at 500 draws and -1069.054 at 2000; with random shifts the error at fixed parameters averages -0.02 at 500 draws and -0.008 at 2000 (standard deviation over seeds 0.14 and 0.027). Scrambled fits therefore give different estimates than before. New fits have draw_version 4; fits with an earlier draw_version still predict with the “mixed” draws they were estimated with. Prediction intervals with scrambled = TRUE keep the “mixed” sequence, which uses one point set and no per-unit blocks.
  • countreg_rp() now uses method = "BFGS" by default (it was "BHHH"). With the analytic gradient, BFGS reached the maximum in each of six test models. BHHH failed on two of the six. On a 500-draw NB2 model with three random parameters it was still at -1093 after 200 iterations, while BFGS reached -1065.5 in about 10 s. On the same model with 100 draws it reported convergence at the Poisson boundary (ln(alpha) = -167), 0.08 below the maximum, where no gradient method can recover. BHHH remains available and is often faster on simple models. Code that relies on the default can give different estimates; pass method = "BHHH" to reproduce earlier fits.
  • Fitted objects no longer keep the optimizer’s log-likelihood function (maxLik::objectiveFn(fit$model) is unavailable): its closure held the data, design matrices and draws, so fits were several times larger than the data (30 MB for 4.3 MB of data).
  • Fitted objects have class c(<estimator>, "flexCountReg"), with <estimator> one of countreg, countreg_rp, renb, poislind_re, repois and negmultinom. The unused S4 class definition is removed. The training data are stored once (obj$data); obj$model$data is gone.
  • regCompTest() with two models now treats the model with fewer parameters as the restricted model (before: the one with the higher log-likelihood), errors when the models were fit to different numbers of observations, and warns when the restricted model has the higher log-likelihood. Its base and null models use the same rows, offset and weights as the fitted model. McFadden’s R^2 is computed against an intercept-only Poisson model for every model by default (so it is comparable across distributions); a different baseline family, with or without the mean covariates, can be chosen with basemodel and variables in both regCompTest() and regCompTable().
  • cor2cov() stops (instead of warning and returning NULL) on invalid input, and checks that C is a symmetric correlation matrix.
  • Probit underreporting now uses P(reported) = pnorm(z’g), the same sign convention as logit (a positive coefficient means more likely to be reported). Previously probit used 1 - pnorm(z’g), so probit coefficients had the opposite sign. Refit probit models to update them; predict() on probit fits made with earlier versions still uses the old convention.
  • countreg(): giving an offset both with offset() in the formula and with the offset argument is now an error. Before, a formula offset() was silently ignored.
  • countreg(): an invalid method, family, stderr or underreport_family is now an error instead of a warning or a silent fallback. dis_param_formula_1/_2 given for a parameter the family does not have is an error.
  • countreg() starting values now come from a Poisson GLM that uses the same rows, offset and weights as the model, so results can differ slightly (usually closer to the optimum).
  • predict() errors when an offset column used in fitting is missing from newdata, instead of silently setting the offset to 0.
  • countreg_rp(): heterogeneity in means now follows Wood and Gayah (2025, Eq. 2). Each random parameter has its own coefficient for each variable in het_mean_formula (named HetMean:<parameter>:<variable>), and the effect is additive (on the log scale for lognormal parameters; multiplicative for gamma parameters, whose mean must stay positive). Previously a single coefficient vector multiplied every random parameter’s mean. Estimates from models with het_mean_formula change; saved fits still predict with their original specification.
  • countreg_rp(): uniform random parameters now span mu +/- St.Dev (draws 2u - 1), matching the paper and the Exact prediction. Previously the draws spanned mu +/- St.Dev/2, so estimated uniform St.Dev values are now half as large. predict() converts saved uniform fits automatically (with a one-time message).
  • countreg_rp(): rpardists is matched to the random parameters by name (not position) and validated. An intercept in both formula and rpar_formula (an unidentified model) is an error; the intercept implied by rpar_formula is not a random parameter unless the fixed formula has no intercept. An invalid panel_id, family or method is an error.
  • countreg_rp(): weights now weight the panel log-likelihood (frequency weights for whole panels) instead of each row’s probability.
  • countreg_rp(): the mixing distribution of PLN, PGE, PLL and PW families uses its own Halton dimension; it previously reused the first random parameter’s draws, which made the two perfectly correlated.
  • predict(method = "Exact") returns Inf (with a warning) where the expected value does not exist: lognormal random parameters with a positive x, and gamma random parameters beyond the domain of their moment generating function. The lognormal formula is documented as a Laplace approximation.
  • renb() and poisLind.re() require group_var, and the panels always come from it (a panel_id column in data is no longer used instead). Bootstrapped standard errors resample whole panels instead of rows.
  • pplindLnorm(), qplindLnorm() and rplindLnorm() convert lambda to mean consistently with dplindLnorm() (the extra exp(sigma^2 / 2) factor is removed).
  • dpLnorm(), dpinvgaus(), dpinvgamma(), dplind() and dgwar() are vectorized directly instead of through Vectorize(). Off-support x gives 0 with a warning, and invalid parameters give NaN with a warning.

Bug fixes

  • The Poisson-inverse-gamma density (dpinvgamma() and the PIG family) could take minutes, or effectively hang, when the optimizer tried a small eta. Its log Bessel function took one recurrence step per unit of order, and the order is about 1/eta. Orders above 100 now use the uniform asymptotic expansion (accurate to about 1e-10 there), so the cost no longer grows with the order. A bootstrap refit that took 12 seconds now takes 0.2 seconds.

  • dpinvgaus(), ppinvgaus() and the PIG1/PIG2 families: P(0) was computed as exp(mu / eta * (1 - sqrt(1 + 2 * eta))), which cancels as eta -> 0 (at eta = 1e-16 the Type 1 PMF summed to 20, and ppinvgaus(5, 3, 1e-16) was 18.4), and fits could exploit it to report a positive log-likelihood. It is now exp(-2 * mu / (1 + sqrt(1 + 2 * eta))), which tends to the Poisson value.

  • dsichel() returned -Inf where the log PMF is finite (for example dsichel(500, 500, 1, 1, log = TRUE)), and qsichel() (and so rsichel()) stopped at 10,000 for heavy tails. Bessel functions now come from a log-scale order recurrence, and psichel() and qsichel() evaluate the PMF in one recurrence sweep and search the support in doubling blocks.

  • The inverse-Gaussian draws behind rpinvgaus() cancelled to 0 for large dispersions; the root is now computed as m / (1 + t + sqrt(t (t + 2))).

  • dpoisweibull() and friends with mean_value and sd_value: the shape was searched only in [0.1, 5], so small coefficients of variation were silently given shape 5 (SD 0.229 instead of 0.01 at mean 1). The shape is now solved from the coefficient of variation with an expanding bracket.

  • regCompTable(coefs = FALSE) printed the coefficients anyway, and an unnamed list of models gave a table without model columns (they are now named “Model 1”, “Model 2”, …).

  • cureplot() no longer prints the cureplots messages “Covariate: indvar_values” and “CURE data frame was provided…”, which named the wrapper’s internal objects; other messages are kept. The documentation of n_resamples now says that the red reference limits are drawn whatever its value (they were described as “no bands” at 0).

  • countreg(): offsets given with offset() in the formula are now used in estimation and prediction.

  • countreg(): bootstrapped standard errors are matched to parameters by name. They were previously sorted alphabetically and printed against the wrong coefficients. Failed bootstrap replicates are counted and reported.

  • countreg(): all data (main formula, dis_param_formula_1/2, underreport_formula, offset and weights) are taken from one set of complete cases, so missing values no longer misalign rows. The number of removed rows is reported.

  • countreg(): stderr = "robust" and stderr = "boot" now set the stored standard errors and covariance matrix ($model$vcov, $model$vcov_type), which summary() and margEffTable() use. stderr = "boot" without bootstraps uses 200 replicates. The SE type is stored in $model$stderr.

  • countreg(): parameter values where a distribution’s density fails no longer abort the fit; the likelihood returns NA so the optimizer steps back.

  • countreg(): start.vals must have one value per parameter, and named values are matched by name. $model$converged is now set (with a warning when the optimizer does not report convergence).

  • predict() returns one value per row of newdata, in order, with NA for rows with missing values, instead of recycling shorter vectors. Training factor levels and contrasts are used, so newdata can contain a subset of levels. Coefficients are matched by name.

  • predict() sums multiple offset columns and uses formula offsets.

  • predict() for PLL models now includes the exp(sigma^2 / 2) lognormal mean factor, as it already did for PLN.

  • countreg_rp() now stores its offset, so predict() uses it. Simulated predictions now include heterogeneity in means and variances.

Bug fixes (distributions and panel models)

  • dpinvgaus() and dpinvgamma() are computed on the log scale, so they no longer return Inf or NaN at large counts (e.g. y > 85 with mu = 2, eta = 0.5).
  • r-functions (rpLnorm(), rplind(), rplindLnorm(), rplindGamma(), rpge(), rcom()) accept vector parameters, as needed for simulation from fitted models. Mixture families draw the mixing variable per observation.
  • q-functions no longer loop forever at p = 1 (they return Inf), return NaN for p outside [0, 1], and no longer recompute the CDF at every step.
  • dplind(lambda = ) uses lambda (it previously ignored it).
  • The RENB likelihood computes log-gamma differences without cancellation for large means. Previously the likelihood was overstated far from the optimum, and optimizers such as BFGS could converge to meaningless estimates.
  • poisLind.re() starts from a moment estimate of theta instead of an undocumented formula.
  • renb() and poisLind.re() use the same data preparation as countreg(): missing values are removed consistently, formula offsets work (giving both a formula offset and offset is an error), and starting values use the offset.
  • countreg_rp() uses the shared data preparation (formula offsets, missing values, numeric weights), starts gamma random parameters from a positive mean, averages panel likelihoods over draws on the log scale, and reports convergence.
  • predict(method = "Exact") for countreg_rp() includes heterogeneity in means and variances.

Further bug fixes and changed results

Changed results are marked (changed).

  • Weights for the panel estimators. renb() and poisLind.re() accept weights, as countreg() and countreg_rp() do. In panel models these are frequency weights of the panels (constant within a panel): a panel with weight w counts as w independent panels in the log-likelihood, the robust covariance, BIC and the bootstrap. Fits with weights equal fits to the expanded panels.

  • Frequency-weight bootstrap (changed). With weights, bootstrap standard errors now draw new frequencies from Multinomial(sum(w), w / sum(w)) and refit with them in place of the weights. This equals the bootstrap of the expanded observations (or panels). Before, rows were resampled with their original weights, which is a different and much more variable sampling scheme. Bootstrap standard errors need whole-number weights; use stderr = "robust" for other weights.

  • Bootstrap acceptance. A replicate counts only if its refit reports convergence (unknown convergence is a failure), has exactly the expected coefficients and finite estimates. Failures are stored by reason in model$boot_failures.

  • Likelihood-ratio tests. Fits store evidence of their analysis sample (rows, response, weights, offsets, panels and the variables they use). An LR test between two models requires the same sample (shared variables must agree row by row), reported convergence for both, nested designs (checked by column space, so equivalent bases such as x and 2 * x are accepted) and matching random-parameter distributions and correlation. A larger model whose log-likelihood is materially below the restricted one’s (LR below -max(0.01, 2e-6 |logLik|)) gives no test, with a reason in LR_reason, instead of LR = 0. The intercept-only base model of regCompTest() is not nested in a model without an intercept. Objects from older versions get no LR test between fitted models (refit them).

  • Mixture families (changed). The PLN, PGE, PW and PLL probabilities are computed on the log scale by deterministic adaptive quadrature over the log of the mixing variable (engine = "quadrature", the new default of the d/p/q functions, countreg() and countreg_rp()). Averaging over 1500 Halton draws was badly biased in the tails: for PGE with shape 1 (geometric with mean 1) and y = 1000 it gave log P = -3847 instead of -693.8. The new values agree with exact special cases (PGE with shape 1 and PW with alpha 1 are geometric; P(Y = 0) of PGE is a beta function) and with independent quadrature to about 1e-9, for counts up to 1e5. Fits are faster too. engine = "halton" keeps the earlier method, and objects without a stored engine predict as before.

  • Moment existence. Random-parameter predictions decide whether E[exp(x beta)] exists from the parameters alone, so Simulated predictions with lognormal parameters no longer need lamW. Exact uses log-scale MGFs and reports an overflow of a finite expectation as such. For lognormal parameters with x < 0, Exact uses a Laplace approximation (documented as approximate).

  • Distribution contracts. Invalid parameters give NaN for that element, with one warning (base R’s convention), and missing parameters NA, at every q including q < 0 and q = Inf (before, those endpoints returned 0 or 1). dgwar()/pgwar() no longer stop for an invalid element. plindley() computes both tails directly.

  • COM controls. find_lambda_cpp() honors its tolerance (relative error of the mean) and iteration limit and reports non-convergence instead of accepting a collapsed bracket; find_lambda_diag_cpp() gives the residual, iterations and status. Unused controls of the internal moment functions were removed.

  • renb(): the log-likelihood is computed as three stable differences of log-gamma functions. For large a and b, terms of size ~1e200 canceled and the optimizer could report a positive log-likelihood of ~1e203 (changed, fits that hit this region).

  • renb() standard errors (changed). renb() now has analytic scores, so its Hessian is the derivative of an exact gradient. Before, it was a second finite difference of the log-likelihood, which was inaccurate (it could be indefinite and give NaN standard errors or delta-method marginal-effect standard errors, notably for ln(a-1) and ln(b)). Estimates are unchanged; standard errors can change.

  • rpardists values are checked before a single value is expanded.

  • Documentation: the PGE equations use one rate convention and explain why the rate cancels; fitted objects carry a schema version (model$fcr_schema).

  • PGE and PW: with the mean parameterization, the scale of the mixing distribution cancels out of the likelihood, so it was not identified (the PMF is identical for every scale). These families now estimate only the shape parameter (one fewer parameter, so AIC and BIC change), and dis_param_formula_2 is an error for them. Predictions from fits made with earlier versions are unchanged. The dpge()/dpoisweibull() families of functions keep their scale arguments.

  • Underreporting is binomial thinning of the true counts, and the model of the reported counts now matches it: for NB1 and PIG1 the reported counts’ dispersion is p * alpha, and for NBP alpha * p^(2 - P) (before, the true-count dispersion was used unchanged, which is not the distribution of thinned counts). Poisson, NB2, PIG2, PIG and the mixed-Poisson families (PLN, PL, PLG, PLL, PGE, PW, SI) were already exact. GP1, GP2, COM and GW are not closed under thinning, so underreporting is now an error for them. This changes NB1, NBP and PIG1 underreporting estimates (changed).

  • Underreporting identification: an intercept-only underreport_formula is an error (only exp(b0) * p is identified), and countreg() warns when the reporting and count coefficients are nearly collinear (correlation above 0.99), which happens when reporting is separated from the count mean only by the curvature of the link function.

  • Likelihood-ratio tests are reported only for valid nesting. summary() no longer reports a test against Poisson for PL, PLG and PLL (which cannot reduce to Poisson: their variance is at least mu + mu^2 / 2), for NBP, SI, PW, PGE and GW (nonregular restrictions), or for boundary families with a dispersion formula. regCompTest() uses the same rules (same estimator and model components, nested parameters and families), uses a 50:50 chi-square mixture when one parameter is on the boundary (also with extra mean covariates), requires two fitted models to use the same observations, outcome, offsets and weights, returns LR_type, and gives no p-value (instead of 1) when the larger model has the lower log-likelihood. The README zero-inflation example now compares models by AIC and BIC.

  • Likelihoods use log-probabilities computed on the log scale (every family density has a log argument), so extreme counts keep finite log-likelihoods (log P(Y = 1000 | mu = 1) = -5913 instead of log(0)). Rows or panels with zero weight contribute exactly 0.

  • The Conway-Maxwell-Poisson functions use the log normalizing constant (it overflowed for lambda = 1000, nu = 1, so dcom(1000, lambda = 1000, nu = 1) was 0 instead of 0.0126), one support rule for the PMF, CDF, quantiles and moments, moments computed from the normalized PMF, and a bracketed solver for the rate given the mean (accurate to about 1e-8, NaN with a warning when it fails, instead of silently returning an unconverged value).

  • Correlated random parameters with three or more parameters: the Chol: labels and the default starting values were built row by row while the Cholesky factor was filled column by column, so labels were attached to the wrong elements, named starting values went to the wrong elements, and the default start was a singular matrix instead of 0.1 * I. Labels, starting values, the likelihood and predictions now use one packing. Estimates and predictions of earlier fits were internally consistent; only their labels were wrong.

  • countreg_rp() rejects a variable in both formula and rpar_formula when its random parameter is normal, uniform or triangular (only the sum of the fixed coefficient and the random mean is identified). Lognormal and gamma random parameters with a fixed shift are still allowed.

  • Auxiliary formulas (distribution parameters, underreporting, random parameters, heterogeneity) keep their trained terms, so data-dependent bases such as poly(), splines::ns() and scale() are evaluated with the training values at prediction time (a row is predicted the same alone or in any batch).

  • Bootstrapped standard errors use only replicates whose refit converged and gave finite estimates for every parameter (failed optimizations were counted as successes before). The warning about failed replicates gives the reasons, the counts are stored (boot_failures), and the covariance uses the accepted replicates only (not pairwise deletion).

  • Frequency weights now give the same results as expanding the data: the robust (sandwich) covariance uses sum(w s s’) instead of sum(w^2 s s’), and BIC uses the sum of the weights (of rows, or of panels in panel models) as the sample size. countreg_rp() weights that vary within a panel are an error (they were silently replaced by the first weight of the panel).

  • All count p-functions (pplind(), ppinvgaus(), ppinvgamma(), ppLnorm(), pplindLnorm(), pplindGamma(), ppge(), ppoisweibull(), psichel(), pgwar(), pcom()) follow one contract: NA gives NA (it gave 0), q < 0 and -Inf give 0, Inf gives 1 (several gave 0 or failed with “result would be too long a vector”), the upper tail and log scale follow, and zero-length input gives numeric(0). Small upper tails are summed directly on the log scale instead of taken as 1 - CDF.

  • cureplot() uses the rows used in estimation by default, builds the outcome, predictions and plotting variable with one mask of complete rows (they could be misaligned after missing values), errors for an unknown indvar, and passes method only to random-parameter and negative multinomial models (the default NULL uses the estimator’s default).

  • Input checks before optimization, shared by all estimators: the response must be finite, non-negative whole numbers (non-integer counts are now an error, not a warning); design matrices must be finite after formula transformations (e.g. log() of a non-positive value) and of full column rank (aliased columns are named); weights must be finite with a positive total; start.vals must be finite; max.iters and ndraws must be whole numbers.

  • Random-parameter predictions: Simulated predictions now report a nonexistent expected value (lognormal coefficient with positive x, gamma coefficient beyond its MGF domain) like Exact predictions, instead of a finite average of draws. rp_mgf() handles zero-scale lognormal and gamma coefficients exactly and computes uniform and triangular MGFs on the log scale.

  • countreg_rp() has a mix_draws argument for the inner integration of the PLN, PGE, PLL and PW families (default min(ndraws, 200)), so the cost is proportional to ndraws * mix_draws instead of ndraws^2. Scrambled Halton draws are generated from a seed stored in the fit, so predictions reuse the estimation draws and leave the caller’s random numbers unchanged.
